newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE-In Yukon, Jack London sparks racism debate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-In Yukon, Jack London sparks racism debate.

text.p: A controversy has erupted in Canada's Yukon over charges that Jack London, the American author whose adventure stories brought worldwide fame to the frigid territory, was a racist.

London's admirers and some scholars dispute the claims, saying they represent a misguided effort to judge the writer out of context by today's standards of political correctness. Even so, the allegations were enough last month to derail a plan by the territorial capital to name a street after London.

Best known for his classics "Call of the Wild" and "White Fang," London traveled the frozen Yukon almost a century ago as part of the Klondike gold rush. This month marks the 80th anniversary of his death on Nov. 22, 1916.

Controversial even in his day, London was an avowed socialist, a heavy drinker and reputed womanizer. He was just 21 when he ventured north to seek his fortune in the Gold Rush, but one winter holed up in a tiny log cabin near Dawson City in the central Yukon was enough to send him home to California suffering from scurvy.

London failed to strike it rich in the Yukon goldfields, but he did unearth a treasure chest of stories and impressions that he mined for 18 years. He wrote more than 50 books before he died of kidney disease at age 40. His Yukon stories focused on the struggle of men against hostile elements and scholars agree race was an important theme throughout London's work.

The current fuss broke out when the Whitehorse City Council decided in September to rename a city street for the writer at the urging of the local Jack London Society, a group of enthusiasts. Similar projects have been launched in other places connected to the author such as Oakland, California, where London grew up and a square is dedicated in his honor

In Whitehorse, the proposal drew immediate opposition, especially from local aboriginal groups. Joe Jack, chief of the Kwanlin Dun First Nation, said London expressed racist attitudes throughout his life and in his work.

Another resident, businessman Robert Nardi, argued before the city council that London should not be honored because he believed in white superiority. Nardi published in the local newspaper passages from London's letters including several to his friend Cloudesley Johns in 1899. In one of them, London wrote, "The lesser breeds cannot endure." And in another, "I cannot but hail as unavoidable the Black and Brown going down before the White."

Ian Roger, president of the Jack London Museum in Oakland, denounced the charges of bigotry as "absolute twaddle," saying London had great respect for other cultures including Canada's aboriginal peoples. "He admired them. He thought their message and their way of communing with nature was worthy of respect and he treated them with respect," Roger said.

Unwilling to wade into this fray, the Whitehorse city council decided last month to drop the street-naming project without taking sides. "We did that in order to salvage the reputation of Mr. London as well as to respect the concerns of the First Nations Council," Whitehorse Mayor Kathy Watson said. First nations is a term used in Canada to describe Indian or aboriginal people.
The dispute reflects a debate that has preoccupied London scholars for years and recalls recent swings of opinion about other historical figures amid a wave of revisionist critique.

Historian Clarice Stasz at Sonoma State Univeristy in California said that while London might be judged racist by today's standards, clear-cut judgements are difficult. "It's not a pure picture. You can say both yes he was a racist and no he wasn't ... London was a very complex character."

Scholars cite evidence that London believed whites were superior and the races should not mix, so-called racialist ideas that were promoted by leading philosophers and widely embraced around the turn of the century. But he was also sympathetic to other cultures and fought against injustice, and his racial beliefs were not motivated by blind prejudice or hatred, experts said.

"The consensus of London scholars is that he was a conventional man of his age. To use the word racist as it is used today after civil rights and genocide has a very different meaning than back in the 19th century," Stasz said.

Although some Yukon residents are angry at what they see as an effort to tarnish London's reputation, the author himself probably would have relished the current argument. "He would be glad he stirred up controversy ... He loved to provoke debate and get people thinking about important issues," Stasz said.
